outcomes.text: use place value and total value of digits up to hundreds of millions in real life
read and write numbers in symbols up to hundreds of millions in real life situations
read and write numbers in words up to millions for fluency
round off numbers up to the nearest hundreds of millions in real life situations
classify natural numbers as even, odd and prime in different situations
apply operations of whole numbers in real life situations
identify number sequence in different situations
create number sequence for playing number games
appreciate use of whole numbers in real life situations

skills.name: Place value of digits up to hundreds of millions
skills.mastery: Given a whole number up to 999,999,999 the child names the place of any digit (ones to hundred millions), including digits beside zeros, and says which digit sits in a named place. Numbers come from real settings such as a county budget or the number of phone lines.
question_forms: name the place of a digit
which digit is in a named place
how many places a number has

prerequisites.reason: Grade 7 extends the places from millions to hundred millions.
Grouping digits in threes helps to find the place.

skills.name: Total value of digits up to hundreds of millions
skills.mastery: Given a whole number up to 999,999,999 the child gives the total value of a chosen digit (digit times its place), adds the total values of two digits, and writes the number in expanded form. The child does not mistake a digit for its total value.
question_forms: total value of an underlined digit
total values of two digits added
difference between two digits of the same value

prerequisites.reason: Total value needs the place first.
Total value to millions is already known.

skills.name: Read and write numbers in symbols up to hundreds of millions
skills.mastery: Given a number said or written in parts (for example 45 million, 12 thousand and 7) the child writes it in figures with every place filled and zero as a place holder, and reads a figure aloud in groups of three. Numbers up to 999,999,999.
question_forms: read a number aloud in groups

prerequisites.reason: The same idea, with millions as the top group.
The groups of three depend on the place of each digit.

skills.name: Write a number in words (figures to words), up to millions
skills.mastery: The child writes a number up to 9,999,999 in words with British spelling, a hyphen in twenty-one to ninety-nine, and each group (millions, thousands, hundreds) in order. Zeros in a group are not spoken. The design limit for words is millions.
question_forms: choose the words for a figure
write a cheque amount in words
spot the mistake in the words
say the same number two ways

prerequisites.reason: Extends words from 100,000 to millions.
The groups of three give the words.

skills.name: Write a number in figures from words, up to millions
skills.mastery: Given a number in words up to millions, such as "two million and forty-five thousand and seven", the child writes it in figures with zero place holders in every empty place.
question_forms: order two numbers given in words

prerequisites.reason: The reverse direction, now with millions.
Writing groups of three digits with zeros.

skills.name: Round whole numbers to the nearest ten up to hundred million
skills.mastery: The child rounds a number up to 999,999,999 to the nearest ten, hundred, thousand, ten thousand, hundred thousand, million, ten million or hundred million: looks at the digit just to the right, rounds up on 5 or more, and writes zeros in all places after the one rounded.
question_forms: round the same number two ways

prerequisites.reason: The same rule on bigger numbers.
You must name the place to be rounded to.

skills.name: Round large numbers in news, budgets and populations
skills.mastery: Given a real setting (a population, a county budget, a news report) the child chooses the sensible place to round to, rounds the number, and says why the rounded number is only an estimate. Rounding a carried digit (such as 999,500 to the nearest thousand) is included.
question_forms: round the number in a report
why a rounded number is not exact

prerequisites.reason: The rule comes first, the setting second.

skills.name: Classify whole numbers as even or odd
skills.mastery: The child classifies any whole number up to millions as even or odd by its last digit, and knows that sums and products of even and odd numbers follow a pattern (even + even is even, odd + odd is even, even x anything is even).

prerequisites.reason: Even means divisible by 2.

skills.name: Identify prime and composite numbers up to 100
skills.mastery: The child tells prime from composite numbers up to 100 by testing small divisors, knows that 1 is neither, that 2 is the only even prime, and that an odd number is not always prime. The child lists the primes up to 50.
question_forms: pick the primes from a table

prerequisites.reason: A prime has exactly two factors.
Even numbers other than 2 are composite.
Quick tests for 5 and 10 rule out many numbers.

skills.name: Add and subtract large whole numbers (up to 9 digits)
skills.mastery: The child adds and subtracts whole numbers of up to nine digits in a column, regrouping across zeros, and decides whether to add or subtract in a story about money, population or distance. Answers are checked by estimating.
question_forms: sum or difference in a story

prerequisites.reason: Regrouping across zeros is the hard part of large subtraction.
Carrying in several columns.

skills.name: Multiply large whole numbers (up to 3 digits by 3 digits)
skills.mastery: The child multiplies a number of up to 4 digits by a number of up to 3 digits using long multiplication, with the zero place holder in the second and third rows, and by 10, 100 and 1,000 by shifting the digits. The product is checked by estimating.

prerequisites.reason: Extends one more digit in the multiplier.
Estimating catches a missing place holder.

skills.name: Divide large whole numbers (up to 6 digits by up to 3 digits)
skills.mastery: The child divides a number of up to 6 digits by a number of up to 3 digits by long division, with zeros in the quotient where a digit does not fit, writes the remainder as a whole number, and checks by multiplying back.
question_forms: what the remainder means in a story

prerequisites.reason: Extends the dividend by two digits.
Checking by multiplication.

skills.name: Work out combined operations in the correct order (with brackets)
skills.mastery: The child works out expressions of up to three operations with brackets, working brackets first, then multiplication and division from left to right, then addition and subtraction from left to right. Numbers up to 3 digits.
question_forms: put in brackets to make a value
find the mistake in the order

prerequisites.reason: Grade 6 order of operations without brackets.
Multiplication and division before addition and subtraction.

skills.name: Use whole-number operations to solve real-life problems
skills.mastery: The child reads a story with two or three steps (fares, fuel, rent, bags and rows), chooses the operations, works them in order and writes the answer with its unit. Money left, total takings and equal sharing are included.

prerequisites.reason: The steps in a story give an expression to work in order.
Large sums and differences.
Multiplying amounts.

skills.name: Find the rule of a number sequence and extend it
skills.mastery: Given the first four to six terms of a sequence with a constant difference or a constant multiplier, the child finds the rule, continues the sequence, and spots a term that does not fit.

prerequisites.reason: Patterns that multiply.
Patterns that add.
Patterns that subtract.

skills.name: Find a term far along a number sequence
skills.mastery: For a sequence that goes up or down by the same amount, the child finds a distant term (for example the 12th) by first term plus the number of steps times the difference, and does not count the first term as a step.

prerequisites.reason: You need the rule to jump ahead.
Repeated addition is multiplication.

skills.name: Create a number sequence from a rule
skills.mastery: Given a rule such as "start at 5, add 4" or "multiply by 3 then add 3", the child writes the first terms, and makes a sequence of their own for a number game, checking that the terms follow the rule every time.
question_forms: write the terms from a rule

prerequisites.reason: Understanding a rule comes before making one.
Creating an adding pattern.

misconceptions.error: Counts the places from the left end of the number.

example.question: In 407,530,918 which place is the digit 5 in?

misconceptions.cause: Reads the digits left to right like words and numbers the places that way.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer thousands as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Put the number in a place value chart and start counting from the ones on the right.
misconceptions.source: to be confirmed by a teacher (no source yet)

misconceptions.error: Loses a place when a group of three has zeros, or names the ten millions place as millions.

example.question: In 305,000,200 what is the place of the 3?

misconceptions.cause: Reads the numbers in groups but forgets that each group has three places.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer millions as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Write the number under a chart with the headings Hundreds, Tens, Ones for each group.
misconceptions.source: to be confirmed by a teacher (no source yet)

misconceptions.error: Ignores a zero when counting places, so the digits after it move up one place.

example.question: In 70,408,003 which digit is in the millions place?

misconceptions.cause: Thinks a zero is empty space rather than a digit that holds a place.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer 4 as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Colour each zero. Say: a zero is a digit that says there is nothing in that place.
misconceptions.source: to be confirmed by a teacher (no source yet)

misconceptions.error: Gives the digit itself when asked for its total value.

example.question: What is the total value of 7 in 47,300,000?

misconceptions.cause: Confuses total value (digit times the place) with the digit.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer 7 as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Ask: if I had 7 notes of one million shillings, how much money? Write 7 x 1,000,000.
misconceptions.source: to be confirmed by a teacher (no source yet)

misconceptions.error: Writes too many or too few zeros after the digit.

example.question: What is the total value of the 3 in 83,402,115?

misconceptions.cause: Counts the digit as the place name instead of counting the zeros after it.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer 3,000,000 as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: The zeros are the places to the right of the digit. Count them off under the digits.
misconceptions.source: to be confirmed by a teacher (no source yet)

misconceptions.error: Works out the total value of one digit and takes the other digit as it is.

example.question: Add the total values of the 2 and the 5 in 25,000,000.

misconceptions.cause: Applies place value to one digit and forgets the other needs it too.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer 20,000,000 + 5 as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Make a two-row table: digit, place, total value. Fill every row before adding.
misconceptions.source: to be confirmed by a teacher (no source yet)

misconceptions.error: Joins the parts as they are said, with no place holder zeros.

example.question: Write 45 million, 12 thousand and 7 in figures.

misconceptions.cause: Sticks 45, 12 and 7 together as numbers rather than giving each group three places.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer 45,127 as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Draw three boxes for each group (millions, thousands, ones) and fill each with its digits and leading zeros.
misconceptions.source: to be confirmed by a teacher (no source yet)

misconceptions.error: Puts a group in the wrong place, for example thousands written in the hundreds group.

example.question: Write 8 million and 450 thousand in figures.

misconceptions.cause: Writes the thousands figure after the zeros of the thousands group.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer 8,000,450 as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Say the name of the group when you write it: 450 thousand goes in the thousands group.
misconceptions.source: to be confirmed by a teacher (no source yet)

misconceptions.error: Puts a comma or space after every four digits, or reads the number in wrong groups.
misconceptions.cause: Counts the digits from the left in lumps that do not match the places.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer 3456,7890,12 as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Start at the right and count three digits, then a comma, and so on.
misconceptions.source: to be confirmed by a teacher (no source yet)

misconceptions.error: Reads a group that starts with zero (050) as if it were a full three-digit number.

example.question: Write 2,050,300 in words.
example.wrong_answer: two million five hundred thousand three hundred
example.correct_answer: two million fifty thousand three hundred

misconceptions.cause: Reads the digits left to right but does not match them to the group names.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer two million five hundred thousand three hundred as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Say each group of three with its name: 2 million, 050 thousand, 300.
misconceptions.source: to be confirmed by a teacher (no source yet)

misconceptions.error: Swaps the tens and ones when writing the words, such as fifty-seven for seventy-five.
misconceptions.cause: Hears seventy and seventeen the same, or reads the last two digits in reverse.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer one thousand and fifty-seven as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Point to each digit: the left digit is tens (seven tens is seventy), the right digit is ones.
misconceptions.source: to be confirmed by a teacher (no source yet)

misconceptions.error: Leaves out the word hundred in a group, or writes thousand for hundred.
misconceptions.cause: Hears "four" and "four hundred" as the same group.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer three million four thousand as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: The 4 is in the hundred thousands place, so say hundred before thousand.
misconceptions.source: to be confirmed by a teacher (no source yet)

misconceptions.error: Writes the words as numbers side by side without zeros: three million and forty-five gives 345.

example.question: Write "three million and forty-five" in figures.

misconceptions.cause: Writes the numbers in the order said instead of in place value groups.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer 345 as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Draw the three groups and put 3 in millions, nothing in thousands (000) and 045 in ones.
misconceptions.source: to be confirmed by a teacher (no source yet)

misconceptions.error: Writes one zero too few or too many after the thousands number.

example.question: Write "two hundred and fifty-seven thousand and seventy-five" in figures.

misconceptions.cause: Forgets that a thousand group has three digits, so seventy-five becomes 750 or 75.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer 257,750 as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Seventy-five is only two digits, so it needs a zero in front to fill the hundreds place: 075.
misconceptions.source: to be confirmed by a teacher (no source yet)

misconceptions.error: Writes a teen (such as 13) for a ty number (30), because they sound alike.
misconceptions.cause: Mixes thirteen and thirty when listening.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer 13,000 as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Thirteen ends in teen (one ten and three); thirty means three tens.
misconceptions.source: to be confirmed by a teacher (no source yet)

misconceptions.error: Looks at the digit in the place being rounded to instead of the digit after it.

example.question: Round 265,320,847 to the nearest hundred million.

misconceptions.cause: Thinks the digit being rounded decides, not the digit to its right.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer 200,000,000 as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Underline the place, then draw an arrow to the digit on its right: that one decides.
misconceptions.source: to be confirmed by a teacher (no source yet)

misconceptions.error: Always rounds the same way (usually down, by dropping digits) without looking at the next digit.

example.question: Round 18,294,211 to the nearest ten million.

misconceptions.cause: Thinks rounding means cutting off the end of the number.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer 10,000,000 as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Put the number on a number line between the two multiples and see which is nearer.
misconceptions.source: to be confirmed by a teacher (no source yet)

misconceptions.error: Gives only the rounded digit, or replaces the later digits with nothing instead of zeros.

example.question: Round 265,320,847 to the nearest hundred million.

misconceptions.cause: Forgets that the rounded number must still be the same size as the original.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer 3 as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: The rounded number must keep every place. Fill the empty places with zeros.
misconceptions.source: to be confirmed by a teacher (no source yet)

misconceptions.error: Rounds to a nearby place (for example ten million) when asked for the nearest hundred million.

example.question: Round 265,320,847 to the nearest hundred million.

misconceptions.cause: Does not name the place before rounding, so rounds to the one that looks easy.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer 270,000,000 as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Say the place aloud before you start and underline its digit.
misconceptions.source: to be confirmed by a teacher (no source yet)

misconceptions.error: Rounds up a 9 and leaves the digit in front unchanged, so no carry.
misconceptions.cause: Treats each digit separately and does not carry.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer 1,999,000 as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Rounding up means adding one place value: 1,999,000 + 1,000 = 2,000,000.
misconceptions.source: to be confirmed by a teacher (no source yet)

misconceptions.error: Believes a rounded number is the exact one.

example.question: A report says about 270,000,000 lines. Are there exactly 270,000,000?
example.correct_answer: No, it is only a close estimate

misconceptions.cause: Does not see rounding as approximating.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer Yes as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Ask: could the real number be 265,320,847 and still be called 270 million?
misconceptions.source: to be confirmed by a teacher (no source yet)

misconceptions.error: Says money amounts cannot be rounded.

example.question: Can a county budget of sh 18,294,211 be given to the nearest million?

misconceptions.cause: Thinks money always needs to be exact.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer No, money must be exact as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Show a newspaper line that says "about sh 18 million". Exact amounts are for accounts, round ones for reports.
misconceptions.source: to be confirmed by a teacher (no source yet)

misconceptions.error: Uses the first digit of the number to decide if it is even or odd.
misconceptions.cause: Looks at the front of the number instead of the last digit.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer even (it starts with 2) as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Only the ones digit tells: 2,357 ends in 7, so one is left over when you share into twos.
misconceptions.source: to be confirmed by a teacher (no source yet)

misconceptions.error: Says zero is neither even nor odd, or that odd + odd is odd.
misconceptions.cause: Zero does not feel like a number to count with.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer neither as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Zero can be shared into two equal groups of zero, and it sits between 1 and -1 in the pattern odd, even, odd.
misconceptions.source: to be confirmed by a teacher (no source yet)

misconceptions.error: Believes every odd number is prime.
misconceptions.cause: Mixes the idea that all primes except 2 are odd with the reverse.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer Yes, it is odd as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Try dividing by 3, 5 and 7: 9, 15, 21 and 27 are odd but composite.
misconceptions.source: to be confirmed by a teacher (no source yet)

misconceptions.error: Counts 1 as a prime number.

example.question: Is 1 a prime number?
example.correct_answer: No, it has only one factor

misconceptions.cause: Remembers that primes can be divided only by 1 and themselves, and 1 fits that.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer Yes as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: A prime has exactly two different factors. 1 has just one.
misconceptions.source: to be confirmed by a teacher (no source yet)

misconceptions.error: Says 2 is not prime because it is even.
misconceptions.cause: Thinks all even numbers are composite.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer No, it is even as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: List the factors of 2: 1 and 2 only. It is the only even prime.
misconceptions.source: to be confirmed by a teacher (no source yet)

misconceptions.error: In subtraction takes the smaller digit from the larger in each column.
misconceptions.cause: Avoids regrouping by reversing the digits that are in the wrong order.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer 223,056,589 as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Show that each column must be top minus bottom; when the top is smaller, regroup from the next column.
misconceptions.source: to be confirmed by a teacher (no source yet)

misconceptions.error: Regroups across a zero but leaves the zero as it was, so the number grows by 10.
misconceptions.cause: Takes 1 from the next digit only once and does not make the zero a nine.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer 3,876,543 as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Break the zeros: 5,000,000 = 4,999,999 + 1. Show the chain of nines.
misconceptions.source: to be confirmed by a teacher (no source yet)

misconceptions.error: Adds or subtracts digits that are not in the same place because the numbers are not lined up from the right.
misconceptions.cause: Lines up numbers from the left.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer 20,000,000 as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Always line up the ones. Use squared paper or a place value chart.
misconceptions.source: to be confirmed by a teacher (no source yet)

misconceptions.error: Leaves out the zero place holder in the second or third row of long multiplication.
misconceptions.cause: Writes the second row directly under the first.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer 1,645 as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: The second row is for tens, so it starts under the tens column. Put a zero under the ones.
misconceptions.source: to be confirmed by a teacher (no source yet)

misconceptions.error: Multiplies by 100 by adding only one zero, or by 1,000 by adding two zeros.
misconceptions.cause: Counts the zeros of the multiplier but loses those already in the number.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer 450,000 as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Shift every digit three places to the left, then fill the gaps with zeros.
misconceptions.source: to be confirmed by a teacher (no source yet)

misconceptions.error: Multiplies by the ones digit of the multiplier only and ignores the tens and hundreds digits.
misconceptions.cause: Treats the multiplier as the last digit only.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer 940 as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Split 124 into 100 + 20 + 4 and multiply by each part, then add.
misconceptions.source: to be confirmed by a teacher (no source yet)

misconceptions.error: Leaves out a zero in the quotient when the next digit is too small to divide.
misconceptions.cause: Brings down the next digit but forgets to write 0 when the divisor does not go in.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer 2,109 as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: After bringing down each digit, write a digit above it, even 0.
misconceptions.source: to be confirmed by a teacher (no source yet)

misconceptions.error: Gives only the quotient when the question needs the remainder, or rounds the remainder away.

example.question: 290 pupils go in buses of 45. How many buses are needed?

misconceptions.cause: Thinks the remainder does not matter.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer 6 as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Draw the buses: 6 are full and 20 pupils are left, so one more is needed.
misconceptions.source: to be confirmed by a teacher (no source yet)

misconceptions.error: Divides the smaller number by the larger when setting up the division.

example.question: A rope 300 m long is cut into pieces of 12 m. How many pieces?

misconceptions.cause: Does not see which number is being shared.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer 0.04 (12 divided by 300) as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Ask: what are we sharing? That number goes inside the division bracket.
misconceptions.source: to be confirmed by a teacher (no source yet)

misconceptions.error: Works every operation from left to right whatever it is.
misconceptions.cause: Reads like a sentence and does not know that multiplication comes first.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer 60 as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Picture 8 shillings and 4 coins of 5 shillings: that is 8 + 20.
misconceptions.source: to be confirmed by a teacher (no source yet)

misconceptions.error: Ignores the brackets and applies the usual order.
misconceptions.cause: Does not see that brackets mean work this part first.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer 28 as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Replace the bracket with its value first: (8 + 4) becomes 12.
misconceptions.source: to be confirmed by a teacher (no source yet)

misconceptions.error: Always adds before subtracting, even when subtraction comes first from the left.
misconceptions.cause: Has learnt that addition beats subtraction, like multiplication beats addition.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer 12 as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Addition and subtraction are equal rank: go left to right. 20 - 5 = 15, then + 3.
misconceptions.source: to be confirmed by a teacher (no source yet)

misconceptions.error: Always does multiplication before division even when the division comes first.
misconceptions.cause: Has learnt a rule that multiplication always goes first.
misconceptions.reveals: The answer 2 as a wrong option, with a reason that names the idea.
misconceptions.help: Division and multiplication are equal rank: left to right. 24 / 4 = 6, then x 3.
misconceptions.source: to be confirmed by a teacher (no source yet)
